The idea that population grows geometrically while food supply grows only arithmetically, so people eventually outrun what they can eat and face famine, is the core claim of the Malthusian view.

Central place theory is about how settlements are spaced according to the population and resources their surroundings can support, so when population outgrows the food a market area supplies, that whole system collapses.

In Florida, natural lakes tied to aquifers and coastal systems carry different dissolved salt levels than stormwater ponds filled by rain runoff, so measured salinity separates the two kinds of water body reliably.

Retention ponds are dug by machines to engineered plans, so their outlines show straight edges, right angles and smooth curves, while natural lakes have irregular shorelines, and that shape difference stands out in spatial data.

Consumers travel to the nearest center offering a good, and settlements arrange into a hexagonal pattern precisely so that everyone's travel distance to services is as small as possible, which is what this theory says.

The rank-size rule describes how settlements of different sizes are distributed, and that distribution arises because people locate so that larger and smaller towns together keep their trips for goods and services short.

Portugal ran the colony through Portuguese-language institutions, and after independence the state pushed one national language through schools and government to unify the country, which kept indigenous languages out of official status.

Large waves of European immigrants arriving in Brazil adopted Portuguese as the common tongue in cities and schools, and that growing mass of speakers is what tipped official status entirely toward Portuguese.

Range is the concept about how far people will travel and how many customers a business can draw, and a store needs enough people inside that range to survive, so it captures the minimum market needed.
Threshold is defined as the minimum number of people needed to support a good or service, so a business below that population cannot stay open, which matches the wording of the question directly.

Hierarchical diffusion means an idea moves down a ranking, from people or places of higher status and influence to those below them, which is exactly the high-to-low social spread described here.
When a high-status person adopts something, followers of lower status copy the underlying idea but adapt it to their own means, and that change in form as it spreads downward is stimulus diffusion.

The model built on range and threshold reasons from an idealized flat plain to a nested hexagonal pattern of market towns, explaining why bigger settlements are fewer and spaced farther apart than smaller ones.

Von Thünen's model starts from an idealized isolated state around one market town, and how far farmers will travel to that market and how much demand it needs shape the spacing of settlements around it.

The area has real hazards like strong currents, sudden storms and busy shipping lanes, and storytelling turned those ordinary dangers into legends of mysterious disappearances, which keeps the place alive as a cultural landmark.

The Gulf Stream through that region carries major fish migrations, and sailors following those schools into rough water generated the lost-ship stories, so documenting the migrations links the ocean science to the folklore.

The semi-periphery sits between core and periphery in the model, with some manufacturing alongside raw-material exports, so a middle level of industrialization is the feature that defines that category.

Semi-peripheral countries are largely rural economies exporting raw materials, with people spread across farmland and villages rather than concentrated in big cities, so the absence of urban centers characterizes them.

New Urbanism designs neighborhoods with mixed uses, narrow streets and shops within walking distance of homes, specifically so that residents can meet daily needs on foot rather than driving everywhere.

A grid of short, connected blocks gives pedestrians many direct routes between any two points, which makes walking practical and neighborhoods self-contained, unlike cul-de-sac layouts that force people into cars.

Dependency theory holds that peripheral regions stay poor because the core extracts their raw materials and controls the terms of trade, which is a direct description of a core economically dominating a periphery.

Sustainable development debates center on the imbalance between rich core regions that consume resources and poorer peripheral regions that supply them, so that framework is about the core's economic dominance over the periphery.

Mediterranean regions get rain spread across the seasons because of the sea's influence, and winters there can turn genuinely cold when northern air pushes south, so steady rainfall with cold winters fits.

Subtropical high pressure sits over these regions in summer and blocks rain, while westerly storms arrive in winter, giving warm dry summers and mild wet winters, the pattern of places like coastal California.
Parks near cities often sit at higher elevations, and visits peak when the high country becomes accessible and stays cooler than the hot lowlands, so elevation drives when the crowds arrive.
Parks close to big metro areas draw heavy day-trip traffic on weekends and holidays when city residents are free, so nearness to urban centers is what shapes when visitation peaks.
By the fourth stage both birth and death rates have dropped and settled at low levels, so natural increase is near zero, which is the mature pattern of most industrialized countries today.
The fourth stage is where improved medicine and sanitation fully take hold, and the death rate drops sharply as a result, which is the change that marks that stage of the model.

Shared environmental threats like floods or storms make people seek protection together, and cities with strong defensive infrastructure pull populations in, so hazards push people toward a common center.
People move toward a city mainly because it offers jobs, higher wages and business openings, and that economic pull is what draws them inward toward the center, making it the main centripetal driver.
The model that describes a city as a set of rings, each wrapped around the central business district and expanding outward as the city grows, is the one built on concentric zones.

Cities grow outward from the downtown core, and as each new belt of development forms it gathers its own smaller centers, which the model with several nodes accounts for while still starting from the central district.
Urbanization is the shift of population from the countryside into cities, and in developing countries that rural-to-urban migration is what has swelled the largest cities into megacities.

Rural migrants arriving in developing-world cities mostly settle on the outskirts, so the city spreads through its expanding fringe, and that growth at the edges is what produces sprawling megacities.

A primate city is defined as one that is disproportionately larger than the next-largest city and dominates national economic, political and cultural life, which matches every part of this description.
A metropolis is the chief city of a country, the mother city in the original Greek sense, so the term names the dominant center of national economy, culture and politics that dwarfs other cities.

Counterurbanization means countering outward sprawl by building upward, concentrating more offices and towers in the central business district so the city grows vertically instead of spreading across the land.
Counterurbanization is the reverse of urbanization, so instead of people moving from countryside to city, they leave cities and move out to villages and rural areas beyond the urban fringe.
Bilateral sideline meetings are where cooperative deals actually get made at the assembly, so a leader who gives a broad speech and then refuses all of them is signaling a turn away from engagement.

Busan is ringed by steep mountains that made it a refuge, and its growth as a retreat, especially when people fled there during wartime, gave it a rapid population surge and a distinct identity.

Busan sits on the southeastern coast facing Japan and the Pacific shipping routes, and its harbor made it the country's main gateway for trade, which drove rapid growth and a distinct maritime identity.
Human geography is the field defined by studying where people live and what they do across the Earth's surface, so the spatial distribution of people and their activities is its core subject.
Geomorphology examines the shape of the land surface, and people and their activities follow those landforms directly, settling in valleys, plains and coasts, so the term covers that spatial pattern.
A greenbelt is a ring of protected open land kept around a city by planning policy, so it marks where urban development stops and countryside begins and keeps sprawl from spreading further.
The exurban line marks the outer edge of commuter development where built-up land gives way to rural land, and planners use it as the limit beyond which urban growth is not permitted.
Retailers locate where customers have money to spend and can reach the store easily, so income levels and access by road or transit decide where shops cluster within a metropolitan area.

Shops need flat, buildable land with easy approaches, and hills, rivers and valleys channel roads and development, so the physical terrain determines where retail can actually locate within a metro area.
High-order goods like specialty stores and hospitals need large thresholds and long ranges, so they locate in the biggest central places, and at the top of that hierarchy sits the city.

Every settlement in the theory is a node, and the hamlet is the basic building block the whole hexagonal network is organized around, so it is the primary node from which the hierarchy of goods is built.

When wealthier households move in and push up property values, the original residents are priced out and leave for cheaper suburbs, and that outward displacement of longtime residents is suburban flight.
Gentrification is when higher-income newcomers move into an older neighborhood, renovate and drive up property values and rents, so the longtime lower-income residents can no longer afford to stay.

White flight is the term for middle-class families leaving city neighborhoods for the suburbs, a move driven largely by the pursuit of better-funded schools and perceived safety, which matches the description.

Urban renewal programs cleared older city housing and built highways that made suburbs reachable, which drove middle-class families outward toward better schools and safer streets, so the term covers that whole movement.
Centrifugal forces push outward from the center, so in a state they are the things that divide it, like ethnic tension, separatism or language divisions that weaken national cohesion.
Centrifugal forces push activity outward from the capital, and policies drawing foreign investment into the interior spread economic power away from the center toward other regions of the country.

World-Systems Theory splits the global economy into a core, a semi-periphery and a periphery linked by unequal exchange, which is exactly the three-part division based on interdependence described here.

The Malthusian view ties population pressure to resources, so the world sorts into regions with food surplus, regions in between, and poor regions dependent on the others, a three-tier division built on interdependence.
Inland states sit far from the warm and cold ocean currents that shape coastal climates and fisheries, and that lack of current influence is what pushed them toward farming instead of maritime trade.
Situation describes a place's location relative to other places, and an inland state far from the coasts and ports naturally turned to farming its land rather than trading by sea.

Seas generally lie off the main through-routes, while the open oceans carry the major commercial shipping lanes between continents, so the absence of those trunk routes is what marks a body of water as a sea.
A sea is a smaller body of saltwater partly enclosed by land and lying close to coastlines, which is why maritime law treats it in terms of the surrounding coastal states, unlike the open ocean.
Mixed-use development describes how compatible uses group together in particular districts of a city, so shops, offices and housing cluster in the zones planned for them.
Functional zoning sorts a city into areas by function, like residential, commercial and industrial, so similar land uses end up grouped together in their own designated zones.
A core-periphery pattern shows up inside cities, with a dense central core and outer belts of lower intensity, so the model explains how cities grow outward in concentric bands from their center.
The model divides space into a wealthy, powerful core and a poorer, dependent periphery, so it explains why wealth and political power are distributed unequally across places.
This model says a city grows around several separate centers, such as a port, a university or an industrial district, rather than one downtown, which is precisely the idea of independent nodes.

The sector model breaks the city into separate wedges, each with its own function and growth path along transport lines, so the layout comes from several distinct units rather than a single central core.
New Urbanism plans compact neighborhoods with sidewalks, bike routes, mixed uses and transit stops, deliberately designed so people can get around without relying on cars.

Planned suburbs were laid out deliberately as designed communities with bus routes, commuter rail stations and sidewalks linking homes to town centers, so intentional design for transit and walking describes them.

The Burgess model pictures the city as rings around the central business district, moving outward through a transition zone and residential belts to the commuter zone, so concentric rings are its defining form.

The sector model still radiates outward from the city center, with land uses spreading out in successive bands along transport routes, so it describes a city emanating from its center in layered zones.
In many countries the capital is the political city while the leading commercial city sits just below it in size, and that second-ranked economic center is what the term primate refers to.
A primate city is far bigger than the next city down and towers over every other urban center in population and influence, and that outsized lead is the defining trait of the term.

Rural Canadian communities rise and fall with mining, forestry and energy, so tracking where natural resource deposits lie explains where people stay in the countryside and where they leave for cities.

The shift from rural to urban living is literally people moving, so net migration measured for each census subdivision shows which rural places are losing residents and which urban areas are gaining them.
A node is the point a service operates from, and its reach is how far out from that node customers will come, so nodal reach names the furthest distance a person will travel to use it.
Range is the maximum distance people are willing to travel to obtain a good or service, beyond which they go elsewhere or do without, which matches this definition directly.

Washington was created specifically as the seat of the federal government, housing Congress, the White House and the Supreme Court, which is a function no other American city holds.
The federal city's heavy concentration of government contracts, defense research and data infrastructure has made it a major tech hub, and that role sets it apart from other large American cities.
The Hoyt model shows cities growing outward in wedges along transport routes, so high-income or industrial sectors extend from the center in pie-shaped slices, which is the pattern described here.

The Burgess model divides the city into zones that extend outward from the central business district, and each zone forms a band of one particular land use, which reads as a series of sectors spreading from the core.
River valleys in the Tennessee basin stay moist and are broken up by water, so settlements placed along the channels and wetlands were shielded from the wildfires that swept drier upland forest.
Where rivers in the basin came together they laid down broad, fertile floodplain soils that suited corn, beans and squash, so the major towns grew up at those river junctions.
Greenfield refers to land that is still green, meaning farmland or open countryside with no previous buildings on it, so a greenfield project builds on a site that has never been developed.
Greenfield development aims to bring fresh life into tired urban fabric, and turning old warehouses into apartments is the standard way cities give existing structures a new start as housing.

Poor medical care in the countryside drives people to leave, and the gap in healthcare between rural areas and cities is what pushes families toward urban hospitals, so healthcare quality acts as the push.

A push factor is a condition in the place of origin that drives people out, and persecution by authorities in the countryside is exactly that kind of threat at home that forces people to leave for cities.
Euclidean zoning divides a city into separate districts by use, keeping homes apart from shops and factories, which is the classic single-use separation described in this question.

Performance zoning sets limits on noise, traffic and pollution, and those standards end up keeping homes away from commercial and industrial activity, so it is the tool that separates residential areas from other uses.

Cities grow in rings, and each ring develops its own centers of activity like shopping streets and factories, so the ring model accounts for several distinct centers spread across the urban area rather than one.

The multiple nuclei model holds that a city develops around several separate centers, such as an airport, a university or an industrial park, instead of growing out from one central business district.

During the Industrial Revolution factories pulled workers off the land and onto the edges of growing industrial towns, where housing spread outward, so that settlement around cities was a form of suburbanization.
Urbanization means the movement of people from the countryside into cities, and the Industrial Revolution drove it as factories in towns drew rural workers looking for wages.
The word joins mega, meaning very large, with polis, meaning city, so a megalopolis is simply a giant city, one whose population passes the ten million mark.
A megalopolis is a string of large metropolitan areas that have grown together along a corridor, like the urban belt running from Boston to Washington, so it names a chain of adjacent cities.

Men and women migrate in different numbers and over different distances, which leaves some regions with more of one sex than the other, so the gender gap describes that uneven pattern of who moves where.
In demographic work the gender gap measures how far women trail men in education and employment, such as literacy and share of the labor force, which is the usual focus of development indicators.

Push-pull theory explains migration as negative conditions driving people out of their home area and attractive conditions drawing them to a destination, which is exactly the two-sided mechanism in the question.

The gravity model treats migration as attraction between places, with the destination drawing people in and the origin sending them out, weighted by size and distance, so it captures both forces at once.

Infill means filling the empty parcels around a city with new homes, and much of that open land sits at the urban edge, so building low-density housing there counts as infill development.

The central business district concentrates offices, banks, stock exchanges and major retail at the most accessible point of the city, so its role is to be the commercial and financial center.
A threshold is literally the line you cross to enter somewhere, so in the theory it marks the edge of a city's built-up area, the physical boundary where its service area begins.
Threshold in this theory means the minimum population or number of customers needed for a good or service to be profitable, which is why higher-order services only appear in larger places.

Howard's plan combined the jobs and amenities of the town with the fresh air and open land of the country, ringing compact towns with greenbelts, so its aim was to merge urban and rural living.
Spatial analysis studies how people relate to particular locations, including how they perceive and value them, so the sense of place and the attachment people feel is part of what it measures.
Topophilia literally means love of place, and it names the emotional bond people form with a particular location, which is exactly the sense of place and attachment the question describes.
The total fertility rate is the average number of children a woman would bear over her reproductive lifetime at current age-specific rates, which is exactly the measure the question describes.

Removing a head of government in a parliamentary system rests on the legislature withdrawing its confidence, and a majority of members voting against the chancellor is what ends the government's mandate.

When migrants carry a custom to a new place, locals there see it and adopt a version adapted to their own culture, so the trait spreads through people moving and sparking change, which is stimulus diffusion.
Relocation diffusion happens when people who hold a cultural trait migrate and carry it with them to a new place, so the trait spreads because the people themselves physically move.
In stimulus diffusion the basic idea catches on but the specific form is rejected or changed to suit local customs, so it is the principle that spreads rather than the exact trait.

Stimulus diffusion begins when actual objects like tools or goods are carried into a new region, and seeing those artifacts prompts local people to adopt them, so the movement of the artifacts is the process.
Spatial interaction describes the movement of people, goods and information between places, and it is modeled as depending on how large the places are and how far apart they lie.

Intervening opportunity explains flows between places by what lies between them, since a nearby attractive location absorbs movement, so the size of places and the distance across them shape where people, goods and ideas go.

Ethnoburbs form when immigrants of a particular group choose to settle near one another in suburbs, drawn by shared language, businesses and institutions, so voluntary clustering is what creates them.

Slums are the dense, crowded blocks of apartment housing built quickly to absorb rural migrants, so planned high-density apartments match the packed living conditions that define them.

Slums and shanty towns are unplanned settlements where people build their own homes on land they often do not own, lacking clean water, sanitation and paved roads, which is informal housing with poor infrastructure.
Union territories are mostly small areas like island groups and city enclaves, while states cover large regions, so the size of the land area is what separates the two categories.

Union territories are governed directly by the central government through an administrator, and most lack their own legislature, while states elect assemblies with full lawmaking powers, so legislative autonomy separates them.
Bid-rent theory says central land goes to whoever can pay most for accessibility, and retailers like clothing stores outbid other users for the core, so they all end up clustered downtown.

When similar stores locate together they share foot traffic, let shoppers compare goods easily and draw more customers than each would alone, and those mutual benefits of clustering are agglomeration economies.

Gender scale looks at where businesses serving men or women are located across a city, mapping how barbershops, salons and similar services are distributed, so it captures gendered space in mapped form.
Scale in geography means the level of analysis, from the body and home up to the nation, so the gender scale examines how expectations about gender roles change as you move between those levels.
